title: Images as Numbers: Pixels, Channels and Colour

Hook.voiceover: You paint a square red in your code. You display the image, and the square is blue. Nothing is broken. You have just met one of the most common surprises in computer vision. By the end of this lesson, you will know exactly why it happens.
Hook.on_screen_text: Red in code, blue on screen?

Explain.voiceover: Last time, we saw that every vision task starts with a grid of pixel values. Today we look inside that grid. For a computer, an image is a grid of numbers, and each cell is a pixel. OpenCV loads it as a NumPy array, so everything you know about arrays still applies.

slide.title: An image is a grid of numbers
slide.body: A photo zooms in until single pixels are visible; each square shows a number. Label: NumPy array.

Explain.voiceover: The array has a shape of height, width and channels. Height is the number of rows. Width is the number of columns. Channels hold the colour. A colour image has three channels, and a greyscale image has only height and width.

Each value is usually an eight-bit integer, from zero to two hundred and fifty-five. Zero means none of that colour, and two hundred and fifty-five means the maximum. So a pixel with three zeros is black, and a pixel with three values of two hundred and fifty-five is white.

slide.title: Values from 0 to 255
slide.body: A gradient bar from 0 (black) to 255 (white). Two pixel swatches: (0, 0, 0) = black · (255, 255, 255) = white. Label: uint8

Explain.voiceover: Now the important part. OpenCV stores colour in the order blue, green, red. Most other libraries, including Matplotlib and most deep learning models, expect red, green, blue. If you pass one order to a tool that expects the other, red and blue swap places. So always convert with one colour conversion call when you move an image out of OpenCV.

slide.title: BGR or RGB?
slide.body: Left: OpenCV → B G R. Right: Matplotlib, Pillow, most models → R G B. Middle arrow: cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)

Explain.voiceover: Here is a simple picture. Think of an image as a large egg box with three layers. Each cup holds a number that says how strong one colour is at that spot. OpenCV stacks the layers blue, green, red. Most other tools expect red on top. Every number is correct, but the colours come out wrong.

One more rule. To reach a pixel, you give the row first and then the column. The origin is the top-left corner, and the row number grows as you move down. We do all of this in Google Colab, which is free.

slide.title: img[y, x]: row first
slide.body: Grid with (0, 0) marked at the top-left. Arrow right: x (column). Arrow down: y (row). One highlighted pixel labelled img[y, x].

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's try it. Hiroshi Tanaka checks photos of ceramic tiles at a small factory in Osaka, Japan. Before he trains any model, he wants to understand his data.
Demonstrate.stock_query: rows of ceramic tiles close up

Demonstrate.voiceover: He opens Google Colab and creates a new notebook. Then he clicks the folder icon on the left and uploads one photo, called tile dot j p g. Menus in Colab change, so follow the idea rather than the exact screen.
screen_steps: Open colab.research.google.com and create a new notebook
Click the folder icon in the left panel
Upload tile.jpg and show it in the file list

Demonstrate.voiceover: He pastes a short cell. It loads the photo with OpenCV, prints the shape and the data type, and prints the top-left pixel. Then it paints a block of pixels red, using blue, green, red order, and displays the image with Matplotlib after converting it to RGB.
screen_steps: Paste the code from content.md into a cell: cv2.imread, print shape and dtype, print img[0, 0], set img[50:150, 100:200] = (0, 0, 255), plt.imshow with cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
Highlight the line that sets the block to (0, 0, 255)

Demonstrate.voiceover: The output shows four hundred and eighty, six hundred and forty, three, and the type is u-int-eight. That is four hundred and eighty rows of height, six hundred and forty columns of width, and three colour channels. The top-left pixel shows three numbers, something like one hundred and eighty, in blue, green, red order.
screen_steps: Point to the printed output (480, 640, 3) uint8
Name each number in turn: height, width, channels
Point to the printed top-left pixel values and label them B, G, R

Demonstrate.voiceover: The image shows a red square, as expected. Now he deletes the conversion call and runs the cell again. The square is blue. Matplotlib read the first channel, which is blue, as red. He puts the call back.
screen_steps: Show the displayed image with the red square
Delete the cv2.cvtColor call so plt.imshow(img) receives BGR
Run again and show the blue square
Put the cvtColor call back and run once more

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to read the shape as width and height, because we say screen sizes that way. Arrays are rows first. But careful: the resize function takes width first. Also, if the file is missing, OpenCV returns None instead of an error, so always check.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Shape is height first. Check for None.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, an image is a NumPy array with a shape of height, width and channels, and usually values from zero to two hundred and fifty-five. Second, OpenCV uses blue, green, red order, so convert to RGB before you display the image or pass it to most models. Third, index pixels row first, from the top-left corner, and check that the image actually loaded.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Image = array (height, width, channels), uint8 0–255. 2. OpenCV is BGR → convert to RGB. 3. img[y, x], row first from top-left; check imread did not return None.
